subject: physics

moments.title: Rutherford's nuclear atom
moments.body:
Rutherford proposes (1911) the nuclear atom: a tiny dense positive nucleus surrounded by electrons at relatively huge distances. The model has a problem: classical electromagnetism predicts orbiting electrons should radiate energy and spiral into the nucleus within nanoseconds. Atoms shouldn't exist at all.

Niels Bohr arrives in Manchester from Denmark in 1912 and takes up the problem.
moments.takeaway: The Rutherford atom is unstable by classical physics. Something new is needed.

moments.title: Bohr's three-part paper
moments.body:
Bohr publishes three papers in the Philosophical Magazine. He proposes:
(1) Electrons in atoms can occupy only specific 'stationary' orbits with quantised angular momentum (n × h-bar).
(2) Electrons in these orbits do NOT radiate, classical electromagnetism notwithstanding.
(3) When an electron jumps from a higher orbit to a lower one, a photon of frequency f = (E1 - E2)/h is emitted.

The model reproduces the Rydberg formula for hydrogen's emission spectrum exactly: 1/λ = R(1/n1² - 1/n2²), with R = 1.097 × 10 to the 7 per metre.

quote.text: How wonderful that we have met with a paradox. Now we have some hope of making progress.

moments.takeaway: Quantisation is in. Hydrogen's spectrum is explained quantitatively. The classical picture of orbits is on borrowed time.

moments.title: Nobel Prize
moments.body:
Bohr wins the 1922 Nobel Prize in Physics 'for his services in the investigation of the structure of atoms and of the radiation emanating from them'. He is 37.

The Bohr model is celebrated as the first quantum theory of an atom. It also has obvious limitations: it works for hydrogen but not for helium or anything heavier. The exclusion principle, electron spin, and ultimately the full quantum mechanics of Heisenberg, Schrödinger and Dirac will be needed to handle the rest.
moments.takeaway: Bohr's model is a partial answer that is still recognisable in today's chemistry teaching of 'shells' and 'energy levels'.

moments.title: Bohr's institute, the Copenhagen interpretation
moments.body:
Bohr's Institute for Theoretical Physics in Copenhagen becomes the hub of quantum physics. Heisenberg works there in 1924-1927 developing matrix mechanics; Pauli is a frequent visitor; Schrödinger writes wave mechanics in Zurich but Bohr engages it deeply.

The 'Copenhagen interpretation' of quantum mechanics — measurement, complementarity, wave-particle duality — comes out of these years. Einstein's famous disagreement with Bohr (the EPR paper, 1935) plays out in correspondence and at conferences for decades.
moments.takeaway: Quantum physics' philosophical framework is developed in Copenhagen. Bohr is its presiding architect.

now.title: Atomic structure today
now.body:
We now describe atoms by the Schrödinger equation: electrons occupy orbitals (s, p, d, f) — probability distributions, not classical orbits. The Pauli exclusion principle, spin, and many-electron interactions explain shell filling and the periodic table.

Bohr's 1913 model survives as a teaching simplification. It correctly captures discrete energy levels, the formula for hydrogen's spectrum, and the emission/absorption of photons by quantum jumps — but it's the wrong picture for any atom beyond hydrogen.
now.open_questions: Can quantum chemistry from first principles reach computational chemistry's accuracy for arbitrary molecules? How do quantum effects play out in biological macromolecules at body temperature?

reflection: Bohr's 1913 model worked perfectly for hydrogen but completely failed for helium. The right answer for one atom and complete failure for the next — that's a strong signal that the model captures something deep but is also missing something deeper. How should physics deal with theories that are partly brilliant and partly wrong?
